title: Five remembrances
hook: the Buddha's five: I will age, fall ill, die, be parted from what I love, and my actions are my own (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus, who said to remember, even while you kiss someone you love, that they are mortal. Your line was look a little longer.

Here's a list nobody pins to the fridge. Not the dentist appointment, but the big ones underneath: getting old, getting sick, the people you'll one day lose. That list usually stays folded. Yet one teacher asked people, women and men, householders and monks alike, to take it out and read it. Often. Slowly. Not to frighten themselves, but because, he said, it loosens something. This week has kept endings in view: the view from above, memento mori, Seneca's rehearsal, the hug that counts. The Buddha closes it with his list.
screen: `THE LIST WE DON'T OPEN.` → `READ IT OFTEN.` → `THE FIVE REMEMBRANCES.`

segments.voice: It comes from a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of the Buddha's numbered discourses, book of fives, number fifty-seven. In plain words: One: I will grow old; I can't escape aging. Two: I will fall ill; I can't escape illness. Three: I will die; I can't escape death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: my actions are my own. I am their owner and their heir; whatever I do, good or harmful, that is what I will inherit. The surprise is who it's for. The text says women and men, householders and monks, should reflect on these often. Not just the monastery. Everyone. And it gives reasons. Remembering age softens the pride of youth. Illness, the pride of health. Death, the pride of simply being alive. Remembering parting loosens the grip of craving. Then the fifth turns everything around. The first four are about what will happen to you. The fifth is about what you do. Age, illness, death and parting are not up to you. That may echo the line Epictetus drew earlier this month, though the two come from different worlds and mean different things. In the Buddha's list, the one thing you truly own is your conduct. So the list doesn't end in gloom. It ends in your hands. You can't stop the clock. You can choose what you say at dinner tonight.
screen: `FROM THE BOOK OF FIVES.` · `AGE, ILLNESS, DEATH, PARTING.` · `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST MONKS.` · `THE FIFTH: WHAT I DO.` · then, large: `MY ACTIONS ARE MY OWN.`

segments.voice: Say each one inside, with a whole breath before the next: I will grow old; I will fall ill; I will die; I will be parted from what I love; my actions are my own. If one of them stings, let it, and soften the shoulders. Then stay with the fifth, and let it point at one thing you'll do today.
Five remembrances. Four things that will happen to everyone, and one thing that belongs to you: what you do. Today's word.
Your line: my actions are my own. Four things happen to you; the fifth is yours. Tomorrow: up, and walking.

howItsDone: In some Buddhist communities, including Theravada monasteries and Plum Village practice centers, the five remembrances are recited aloud as part of a chanting session.

fork.setup: you've just read four remembrances: age, illness, death, parting. what does the fifth one say?
options: so enjoy it while it lasts.
fork.reveal: the fifth turns the list around: I am the owner and heir of my actions. the first four aren't up to you; this one is.

original.note: Pali, kammassako: owner of one's actions, from kamma (action). the word inside the fifth remembrance.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy list of bad news.
what it means: four things no one escapes, then one thing you truly own, your actions.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 5.57, in the book of fives, which pairs each reflection with what it weakens: pride, craving, misconduct.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the teach said the Buddha 'adds something of his own' to Epictetus, which reverses history (the Buddha is centuries earlier) and ranks one tradition as building on the other; rewritten as a resemblance between separate traditions. Hook no longer opens 'Most of us... Now picture', and 'monks and parents and farmers' now matches the text's 'women and men, householders and monks'. howItsDone 'many... often daily' softened.

AN 5.57 paraphrased (no public-domain English translation of the Anguttara the writer could quote with certainty). Check the pairing of each reflection with what it weakens: youth-intoxication, health-intoxication, life-intoxication, craving/desire, and misconduct for the fifth.
Pali kammassako (कम्मस्सको), 'owner of kamma': confirm spelling and Devanagari rendering; the sutta's phrase is kammassakomhi.
howItsDone names Theravada and Plum Village recitation; confirm this is fair and not overstated.
The teach's nod to Epictetus (dichotomy of control, days 111–116) is stated as a resemblance only; the traditions are kept separate.
